questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I wanted to go to a place where I could experience some beautiful nature and live in a city smaller than Copenhagen, to feel more connected to the nature and the places around me. I also read about the UniFlats that University of Otago offer, and thought it was really nice to have housing secured before I moved here, as that made it very easy to find a place to live, and gave me less worries.
I also wanted a country that spoke english as I am more confident in that language.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I can highly recommend living in UniFlats through the University of Otago as they made a great match with me and my flatmates, you are sure that you have a place to live, when you arrive in Dunedin, and they are always quick to fix stuff in the flat, if there is anything broken. They are also great at hosting events for international students.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, there is a lot of information on the university's website, and they also sent me a lot of information and hosted webinars when I was signed up to study there.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: In UniFlats there is a KiwiHost, who is a person from New Zealand that live with you and can help you to figure out where to get the right resources for any problem that might occur. UniFlats also have an office and the university have a team called "Campus Watch" that will be quick to help you if you ask.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I simply applied to live in UniFlats through the University's websites, it is a site called "Te Puna" that you go to, to apply for housing, they also have dorms available. But the univeristy will guide you through the housing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: UniFlats always ask people a lot of questions about their preferences and how they want to live, to make sure that they put people together who are like eachother and put them in a location that fits their needs. Castle Street and Leith Street are known to be party streets, so that is good to know if you either want to live there or avoid them. In

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: In UniFlats you will often live with other international students, so if you would rather live with kiwi's it might be worth it to have a look at some facebook groups to see if you can find a flat with some kiwi's. Usually the landlords can be a bit sketchy though, so it might be worth it to live in UniFlats, to make sure you live in a nice house that is maintained properly. All the flats in Dunedin are rather cold and bad insulated, but you kind of get used to layering up. Almost all students live in houses ("flats"), so that is a fun experience. Otherwise you can stay in a dorm.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I had to apply for acceptance at the university, but if KU already gave you permission to go on exchange at that university, the host university will almost always accept you. 
Remember to apply for a visa in good time. 
Have a look at all the papers and make sure you have documentation to show which relevant papers you have taken at home, if you want a paper at the host university with prerequisites.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Webinars, online folders, information on websites, I could e-mail international student guides

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Very succesful, I got the three classes that I wanted in the end. 
Remember, that semester 1 in Denmark is semester 2 in New Zealand and vice versa.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Watch the webinars, and ask questions if you have any.
Don't leave it all to last minute, remember to stay updated every time the university sends out an email.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was satisfied with the courses, although they were taught a bit different from home. This is both a bit difficult, but also a great way to learn about yourself and your own skills.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: In New Zealand the courses/papers are grouped in different levels according to how hard they are, how much knowledge you need before taking them, and what year you are in preferably. First year courses are level 100, second year courses are level 200 and third year courses are level 300. I had one course of each level, and I thought they were all at a reasonable level. The courses that I had the least background knowledge on were the hardest, but I also think that my level 300 course was a bit harder and more time consuming than the other courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In University of Otago they have a lot of practical sessions in each class, which I really liked, as you get to talk about the material from that week in smaller classes. You also have to turn in assignments regularly and the grades for the assignments count towards your final grade for the course. This means that all of my exams are only worth 50% of the total grade of each course. The lectures are also way shorter, and I felt like I had more free time (and time for homework of course).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
MAOR102, Māori Society 
ECOL211, Ecology of communities and ecosystems
MARI302, Biology and behaviour of marine vertebrates

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend taking a class on Māori culture, as it is an important part of New Zealands history and culture. Either "Māori performing arts" where you learn traditional Māori songs and dances, I really regret not taking this course, it seems like a lot of fun, and an easy course. I can also recommend Māori society if you prefer learning about the culture in a classroom. 

Also try to find some courses that have field trips to get out and see the local area too.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
When I went travelling with my friends we had to rent cars becuase the public transport doesn't go a lot of places, so that was a bit more expensive. 
The food is also way more expensive than I thought it would have been. A cucumber can be up to 40 DKK for example.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food in the supermarket was way more expensive, but going out to a restaurant or cafe was cheaper than Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I can really recommend trying to go on some of the Tramping Clubs trips as well as signing up for "AAPES" which is a ecological club that do a lot of volunteering in nature. Otherwise SEA (Students for Evironmental Action), Slow Food club and the Vegan Club were nice to.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The University hosted quiz nights, inter-college competitions, sport-competitions, there is a free gym and group sports at unipolar, there is a free music room at OUSA, where you can play music. Every wednesday there is free breakfast at OUSA, and 4 dollar lunch every day (except weekends) also at OUSA.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend using the free gym at Unipol, and going to all the social events both through the university, UniFlats, and the clubs. I can recommend exploring Dunedin, go to the peninsula, St. Clair beach, Mount Cargill, see glowworms for free at Nichols Creek, get a BeeCard for the bus, it is really cheap to take the bus around Dunedin. Go for adventures and rent or buy a car to se the rest of the county!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go for hikes either in the local area or in the rest of the country. Go to the local Farmers market every saturday in Dunedin. Spend time with your friends and flatmates.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy to adjust to the culture. For me, I just had to adjust to speak and write english all the time, which was a bit hard at first, because almost all of my flatmates were native english speakers, so I felt very insecure about my accent and my vocabulary. But donøt worry! It comes to you easily after some training, and everybody loves a cute danish accent. Otherwise, I love that Dunedin is a student city, so there's a lot of students around all the time and a lot of stuff going on always.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The kiwi's can be a bit hard to befreind, but I can really recommend joining the social clubs and going to their events and volunteering, that helped me get to talk to some kiwi's. Otherwise I of course met them in my classes, but it is a bit hard to talk inbetween lectures, as everyone is rushing to get to their next class. But I made some friends in the practical lessons and if you are braver than me, you can also try and sit next to some of your classmates in the lectures.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I don't think I was really very challenged, except that I didn't know anyone in my classes at first, so I had to think more about socialising in my classes.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Sausage sizzles, friendly kiwi's, student life, partying, going for hikes, enjoying nature, social gatherings through the uni or social clubs.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Get as much money saved up as you can, try and get some scholarships, apply early for scholarships and grants and remember to get a recommendation from a teacher. Just apply for all the scholarships you see, it really worked out nice for me!

Apply to live in UniFlats! They are great. 

Buy some nice tramping boots! If you like nature you will need them.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: People often ask "how are you", and the usual answer is just "Good, how are you", no matter how you feel, don't be thrown off by this funny interaction

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting my wonderful flatmates, learning to be independent in another country, overcoming the troubles that I had with help from my flatmates, learning how strong I am, and how much I can overcome on my own.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Speaking and writing and learning in english. All. The. Time. But I had good periods and worse periods, it is important to know though, that it will always get better again, even if you are feeling a bit challenged at any moment.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go on exchange no matter what!! It's amazing and you grow so much from the experience.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
